summary: Michael Sassano, CEO of Somai Pharmaceuticals in Lisbon, joins Bryan Fields to explain why he sees Europe as a '51st state' opportunity for US cannabis companies, breaking down the EU-GMP framework, the massive regulatory lift required to build pharmaceutical-grade cultivation and extraction facilities, and why so few companies globally hold true EU-GMP status. The conversation covers the looming crackdown on 'EU-GMP washing,' the vertical-integration race across European clinics, pharmacies and distribution, and how US rescheduling could reshape the trans-Atlantic cannabis trade. It's a practical look at building pharmaceutical infrastructure years before a market fully matures.
takeaways: Michael Sassano frames Europe as a '51st state' — a roughly 3.5 billion euro market that a single EU-GMP grow and manufacturing footprint can service across multiple countries.
Only an estimated 65-90 EU-GMP licensed cultivators/manufacturers exist globally, versus thousands of licensed grows in the US and Canada, creating a severe supply bottleneck.

Building a true EU-GMP facility typically takes 3-4 years (Somai did it in 1 year 8 months); launching a single new product under GMP can take up to two years due to equipment qualification and stability testing.

Owning an in-house lab lets Somai self-validate products and generate its own EU-GMP Certificates of Analysis, saving millions versus outside labs and enabling hundreds of product SKUs instead of just a handful.

Regulators are cracking down on 'EU-GMP washing,' where non-GMP flower is reprocessed or restamped as GMP; Germany leading a shutdown of this practice could spike EU-GMP flower prices and risk pushing patients back to the black market.

Vertical integration in Europe spans grow, manufacturing, distribution, clinics, and pharmacies in each country — companies that don't control the full chain face margin compression as GMP supply tightens and buyers gain leverage.
Europe's cannabis pharmacopoeia requires full-bud flower (no trim) and made-from-scratch ingredients, unlike the US market's trim-based extraction and off-the-shelf flavoring components.

Somai's 2026 strategy avoids chasing discounted commodity markets, instead prioritizing EBITDA, proprietary product edges (like its AeroMDR vaporizer), and selective, cost-effective expansion into smaller EU countries.

faq.question: Why does Michael Sassano describe Europe as the US cannabis industry's '51st state'?
faq.answer: Because a single EU-GMP cultivation and manufacturing operation can legally service multiple European countries at once, acting like one vertically integrated state with different sales points — an estimated 3.5 billion euro market, which he says could rival or exceed a state like Rhode Island in value.

faq.question: What is EU-GMP and why is it so scarce?
faq.answer: EU-GMP (European Union Good Manufacturing Practice) is the pharmaceutical-grade certification required to manufacture and distribute cannabis medicines across EU countries. Only an estimated 65 to 90 cultivators/manufacturers worldwide hold it, compared to thousands of non-GMP grows in Canada and the US, making it a scarce, highly coveted status.

faq.question: How long does it take to build an EU-GMP cannabis facility and launch a product?
faq.answer: The average build time for a facility is three to four years; Michael Sassano's company did it in one year and eight months during COVID. Launching a single new product on top of that can take up to two years due to equipment qualification, validation batches, and stability testing.

faq.question: What is 'EU-GMP washing' and why are regulators cracking down on it?
faq.answer: EU-GMP washing is the practice of taking already-dried, non-GMP flower and reprocessing or repackaging it at a GMP facility just to stamp it as EU-GMP certified. Regulators, particularly in Germany, are shutting this down because it misrepresents the product's actual manufacturing standard, and a crackdown could sharply tighten EU-GMP flower supply and raise prices.

faq.question: Why does Somai Pharmaceuticals operate its own in-house testing lab instead of using third-party labs?
faq.answer: Owning the lab lets them self-validate products, generate their own EU-GMP Certificates of Analysis, and satisfy strict regulators who want direct ownership of data. It also saves enormous cost — a single product validation can cost tens of thousands of dollars, and building a full portfolio of hundreds of stability-tested SKUs would cost millions through outside labs.

faq.question: How does vertical integration work differently in European cannabis markets compared to the US?
faq.answer: In the US, product typically flows directly from grower to dispensary. In Europe, it moves from grow to a country-specific distribution license, then to a prescribing clinic, and then to a pharmacy that dispenses it — each step can take a margin cut unless a company owns the clinic, distribution, and pharmacy itself, as companies like Curaleaf and Aurora have done in certain markets.

faq.question: Could the internal, pharma-style lab testing model used in Europe come to the US cannabis industry?
faq.answer: Michael Sassano says it's possible if the FDA takes a strict pharmaceutical stance on cannabis, which he thinks is unlikely to fully happen, but if it did, companies would need GMP-grade equipment, standards, and the ability to file formal medical dossiers with the FDA, similar to the European model.

faq.question: Why doesn't Somai Pharmaceuticals use trim in its extraction process?
faq.answer: The EU pharmacopoeia has no defined derivation for trim, so Somai extracts only from full-bud flower using single-strain batches, which allows them to prove strict batch-to-batch consistency required by serious regulatory markets.
